power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: A mixed analysis of variance yielded a main effect of probe channel, F(1, 15) = 13.22, p = .002, partial² = .47, η with faster responses to probes in the attended ear.
The main effect of defensive group was not significant, F(1, 15) = 0.254, p = .622.

The within-group interaction for repressors did not reach the conventional .05 level, F(1, 9) = 4.00, p ≈ .077, partial² = .31.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≈ .077", Text = "The within-group interaction for repressors did not reach the conventional .05 level, F(1, 9) = 4.00, p ≈ .077, partial² = .31."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .622", "p ≈ .077"), Sentence = c("The main effect of defensive group was not significant, F(1, 15) = 0.254, p = .622.", "The within-group interaction for repressors did not reach the conventional .05 level, F(1, 9) = 4.00, p ≈ .077, partial² = .31." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: From Tone Probes to Dot Probes: The Development of an Auditory Procedure for Studying Emotional Attentional Bias

text.text: The study of emotional influences on cognition has been transformed by experimental methods that permit inferences about processing without requiring participants to describe or evaluate emotionally significant information directly.
One widely used family of methods presents information at competing locations or channels and measures the speed or accuracy of responses to nominally neutral probes.
Differences in probe performance are then interpreted, subject to appropriate assumptions, as evidence about the allocation of attention (Bar-Haim et al., 2007; Yiend, 2010).
text.formatted: Differences in probe performance are then interpreted, subject to appropriate assumptions, as evidence about the allocation of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bar-Haim et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Yiend, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The most influential application is the visual dot-probe procedure reported by MacLeod, Mathews, and Tata (1986).
text.formatted: The most influential application is the visual dot-probe procedure reported by MacLeod, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Mathews, and Tata (1986)</ref>.

text.text: Their participants viewed competing words and responded to visual targets appearing at locations previously occupied by those words.

The task has subsequently supported a substantial research programme on threat-related attention in clinical and nonclinical populations, while also generating important debates about the reliability and interpretation of attentional-bias indices (Kappenman et al., 2014; McNally, 2019).
text.formatted: The task has subsequently supported a substantial research programme on threat-related attention in clinical and nonclinical populations, while also generating important debates about the reliability and interpretation of attentional-bias indices <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kappenman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">McNally, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The development of this method also has an auditory history.

In an undergraduate dissertation submitted at University College London in 1981, I described and implemented a modified dichotic-listening experiment in which reaction times to brief, emotionally neutral tones were used to examine attention between competing speech channels.
The emotional content of words in the attended channel and a measure of defensive style were the variables of theoretical interest (Halkiopoulos, 1981).
text.formatted: The emotional content of words in the attended channel and a measure of defensive style were the variables of theoretical interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Halkiopoulos, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: The dissertation, originally submitted under the title Towards a Psychodynamic Cognitive Psychology, is available in the Open Science Framework archive (https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/6y3d8). MacLeod et al. (1986) acknowledged that this unpublished research motivated the development of their visual paradigm.
text.formatted: The dissertation, originally submitted under the title Towards a Psychodynamic Cognitive Psychology, is available in the Open Science Framework archive (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/6y3d8">https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/6y3d8</ref>). <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">MacLeod et al. (1986)</ref> acknowledged that this unpublished research motivated the development of their visual paradigm.

text.text: Subsequent published accounts also placed the auditory study within the intellectual background of the dot-probe method (Eysenck, 1989; Mathews, 1990; Borkovec, 2004).
text.formatted: Subsequent published accounts also placed the auditory study within the intellectual background of the dot-probe method <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eysenck, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Mathews, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Borkovec, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The present article has three purposes.
First, it reconstructs the theoretical and methodological route by which I arrived at the 1981 experiment.
Second, it reports its design and findings in a form accessible to contemporary readers, while explicitly acknowledging the limitations of a small historical study.
Third, it places the auditory procedure in the broader methodological history of attentional probes and considers what this comparison can contribute to current research.
The focus throughout is the scientific development of experimental methods, not the evaluation of individuals or institutions.
>Intellectual background and development of the procedure
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Intellectual background and development of the procedure</head>

text.text: My interest in emotional attention emerged from the New Look tradition, which investigated how motivational and emotional factors might affect perception and recognition.

Particularly important were discussions of perceptual defence and vigilance: the possibility that threatening material might, under different conditions or in different individuals, encounter elevated or reduced recognition thresholds (Byrne, 1961; Dixon, 1971; Erdelyi, 1974).
text.formatted: Particularly important were discussions of perceptual defence and vigilance: the possibility that threatening material might, under different conditions or in different individuals, encounter elevated or reduced recognition thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Byrne, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dixon, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Erdelyi, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: As a psychology student at UCL, I was interested in whether selected psychodynamic propositions could be expressed as testable claims about ordinary information-processing mechanisms.
Norman Dixon supervised the dissertation and provided a particularly relevant intellectual environment.
A central methodological difficulty concerned the interpretation of traditional perceptual-defence findings.

If participants are slower to report a threatening word, is that because less information about it was perceptually processed, because they adopted a different criterion for reporting it, or because they hesitated to produce the response?
Dixon (1971) and Erdelyi (1974) discussed versions of this problem.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dixon (1971)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Erdelyi (1974)</ref> discussed versions of this problem.

text.text: Dixon's earlier work offered an instructive alternative: rather than asking participants to report the emotionally significant stimulus, he measured the threshold for a neutral light signal presented in conjunction with subliminal material of differing emotional significance (Dixon, 1958).
text.formatted: Dixon's earlier work offered an instructive alternative: rather than asking participants to report the emotionally significant stimulus, he measured the threshold for a neutral light signal presented in conjunction with subliminal material of differing emotional significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dixon, 1958)</ref>.

text.text: The general methodological lesson was that an emotionally neutral response might provide indirect evidence about the effects of emotional information.

I approached the same problem through selective attention. Cherry's (1953) dichotic-listening procedure allowed two streams of speech to be presented concurrently while participants shadowed one and ignored the other.
text.formatted: I approached the same problem through selective attention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cherry's (1953)</ref> dichotic-listening procedure allowed two streams of speech to be presented concurrently while participants shadowed one and ignored the other.

text.text: I reasoned that a threat-related change in attention might be detectable as a redistribution of processing between the speech channels.
The challenge was to obtain an index of that redistribution without simply replacing one emotionally laden recognition response with another.
The solution I developed was to introduce short neutral tones into the ongoing dichotic-listening task.
A tone could occur in the ear carrying the shadowed message or in the opposite ear, following a neutral or a threatening word in the attended message.
Participants would press the same response key as quickly as possible whenever a tone occurred, regardless of which ear received it or what kind of word preceded it.
Thus, the response requirement did not refer to the threatening word or vary according to its emotional content.
The key assumption was that probe detection would ordinarily be faster in the attended than in the unattended ear.
If a threatening word prompted a shift of attention away from the shadowed message, that attended-ear advantage should diminish.
If it produced stronger concentration on that message, the advantage should increase.

The theoretical value of the procedure lay in the interaction between the location of the probe and the emotional significance of preceding material, rather than in the response to either factor in isolation.
The dissertation tested predictions derived from contemporary accounts of defensive style.

Individuals classified as relatively repressive or inhibitory were expected to display a reduced attended-ear advantage after threat; those classified as relatively sensitising or facilitative were expected to show an increased advantage.
These were hypotheses about styles of managing threatening information as indexed by Ullmann's (1962) facilitation-inhibition measure.
text.formatted: These were hypotheses about styles of managing threatening information as indexed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ullmann's (1962)</ref> facilitation-inhibition measure.

text.text: They should not be treated as interchangeable with a simple division into high-and low-trait-anxiety groups.
The procedure was implemented in audition for practical reasons: the required dichotic recordings could be prepared with the available technical facilities.
A visual implementation was also conceivable, but it was the auditory experiment that was developed and documented in 1981.
My account of the route to this design is a retrospective reconstruction, whereas the dated dissertation provides contemporary evidence for the procedure and its underlying rationale.

Neutral probes and reaction times had been used to study attention before 1981. Posner and Boies (1971), for example, employed auditory probe responses during an ongoing visual task to investigate components of attention and processing demands. Flaherty and Coren (1974) used reaction time in dichotic listening to compare attended and unattended inputs, including tonal targets. Hink and Hillyard (1976) presented irrelevant auditory probes during attention to competing speech messages and measured selective processing electrophysiologically through evoked potentials.
text.formatted: Neutral probes and reaction times had been used to study attention before 1981. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Posner and Boies (1971)</ref>, for example, employed auditory probe responses during an ongoing visual task to investigate components of attention and processing demands. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Flaherty and Coren (1974)</ref> used reaction time in dichotic listening to compare attended and unattended inputs, including tonal targets. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hink and Hillyard (1976)</ref> presented irrelevant auditory probes during attention to competing speech messages and measured selective processing electrophysiologically through evoked potentials.

text.text: These studies are relevant methodological precedents and demonstrate that individual elements of a probe-based approach were already established.
They did not, however, constitute the intellectual route by which I devised the 1981 experiment: I was not aware of these particular probe studies when designing it.
The distinction matters because methodological precedence and historical influence are separate issues.

The distinctive feature of the 1981 arrangement was the conjunction of competing auditory speech streams, emotional variation in the attended material, neutral lateralised probes, an invariant speeded behavioural response, and predictions about defensive differences in attentional distribution.

The contribution is therefore best characterised at the level of this integrated experimental design and its theoretical application, rather than as the invention of probe measurement in attention research generally.

In correspondence following his reading of an account of the study, Steven A. Hillyard, whose earlier work with Robert Hink provided a close electrophysiological comparison, offered this qualified assessment of the 1981 procedure and expressly authorised its quotation: Your undergraduate study is indeed a cool paradigm, and as far as I know it's the first of its type-using RT to neutral auditory probes as a measure of assessing the direction of auditory attention to speech that includes emotional words.
(S. A. Hillyard, personal communication, October 21, 2026; reproduced with permission.)
Hillyard also noted that the existence of earlier probe techniques does not preclude originality in a different experimental setting.

His assessment is a useful specialist perspective on the distinctiveness of the auditory arrangement, rather than independent evidence of the historical path from the 1981 study to the later visual procedure.
>The 1981 auditory experiment
text.formatted: <head n="3." >The 1981 auditory experiment</head>

text.text: Eighteen undergraduate psychology students began the study; 17 contributed to the reported analysis.

On the Ullmann (1962) Facilitation-Inhibition Scale, administered after the experimental task, 10 were assigned to the relatively inhibitory (here termed "repressor") group and seven to the relatively facilitative (here termed "sensitiser") group.
The more familiar repression-sensitisation terminology of Byrne (1961) is retained to describe the theoretical contrast, although the actual classification instrument was Ullmann's scale.
text.formatted: The more familiar repression-sensitisation terminology of <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Byrne (1961)</ref> is retained to describe the theoretical contrast, although the actual classification instrument was Ullmann's scale.

text.text: The available report does not provide sufficient information for a modern assessment of cut-off selection, recruitment procedures, or statistical power.

The distinction between defensive style and trait anxiety is important for interpreting these groups. Weinberger, Schwartz, and Davidson (1979), for example, distinguished repressive coping from genuinely low anxiety by considering both reported anxiety and defensiveness.
text.formatted: The distinction between defensive style and trait anxiety is important for interpreting these groups. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Weinberger, Schwartz, and Davidson (1979)</ref>, for example, distinguished repressive coping from genuinely low anxiety by considering both reported anxiety and defensiveness.

text.text: The 1981 study instead divided participants using Ullmann's facilitation-inhibition measure alone and did not independently assess trait anxiety or social desirability.

Its results therefore cannot determine whether any group differences arose from defensive style specifically, from correlated differences in anxiety, or from other characteristics associated with the scale.
The historical labels used here describe the original theoretical contrast, not a contemporary diagnostic classification.
Participants heard synchronised pairs of spoken words, one word to each ear, at approximately one pair every 1.5 seconds.
They were asked to repeat aloud the words in a designated ear (the attended channel) while ignoring the other stream.
The ear designated for shadowing was determined at random.
Half the words in the attended stream were emotionally negative and the remainder neutral; all words in the unattended stream were neutral.
A male speaker recorded the material.
Word frequency was considered using the norms of Kučera and Francis (1967).
text.formatted: Word frequency was considered using the norms of <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kučera and Francis (1967)</ref>.

text.text: The main experimental sequence comprised 40 word pairs.

Eight words in the attended channel were followed immediately by a brief, clearly audible pure tone: four designated as neutral (chairs, sale, silver, actor) and four as threatening (grave, fail, cancer, snake).
The tone occurred either in the attended or in the unattended ear, with the probe locations distributed across word types.
Participants pressed one response key as quickly as possible following each tone.
The response was the same for all probes, irrespective of location or preceding word.
The word list included words of differing syllabic lengths; the original preprint's characterisation of all selected words as disyllabic has therefore been removed.
Practice was provided before the main sequence.
The practice materials included an initial shadowing-only block and a further block containing tones; the protocol allowed repeated attempts to achieve accurate shadowing.
The final word lists, recordings, probe duration and intensity, detailed trigger timings, and triallevel responses are not available in the materials examined for the present reconstruction.
No new trial-level analysis has therefore been attempted.

The design crossed a between-participants factor (defensive style: repressor versus sensitiser) with two within-participants factors (tone channel: attended versus unattended; preceding attended-word type: threatening versus neutral).
The first prediction was a general reaction-time advantage for probes delivered to the attended ear.
The second was a three-way interaction: relative to neutral words, threatening words were expected to reduce the attended-channel advantage among repressors and increase it among sensitisers.
Only eight words were probed in the 40-pair main sequence.
If those eight probes were distributed equally across the four combinations of tone channel and word type, each participant contributed just two observations to each condition.
This is a limitation of the historical experimental implementation and makes individual condition means sensitive to trial-level variation.
Table 1 reproduces the response-latency means and standard deviations from the manuscript account of the original analysis.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> reproduces the response-latency means and standard deviations from the manuscript account of the original analysis.

text.text: All values are in milliseconds.

The comparison between attended and unattended tone channels can also be expressed as an advantage score, calculated by subtracting attended-channel reaction time from unattended-channel reaction time.
Table 1.

Mean tone-probe reaction time (SD), by defensive style, preceding attended word, and probe channel Defensive style Attended ear: threat Attended ear: neutral Unattended ear: threat Unattended ear: neutral Repressors (n = 10) 453 (173) 408 (186) 473 (149) 504 (142) Sensitisers (n = 7) 346 (186) 391 (194) 480 (232) 452 (184) Note.
"Threat" and "neutral" designate the immediately preceding word in the attended ear; tone-probe location is indicated by column.
Values are descriptive means from the historical report.
A mixed analysis of variance yielded a main effect of probe channel, F(1, 15) = 13.22, p = .002, partial² = .47, η with faster responses to probes in the attended ear.
The main effect of defensive group was not significant, F(1, 15) = 0.254, p = .622.

The principal predicted interaction among group, channel, and word type was significant, F(1, 15) = 8.99, p = .009, partial² = .37 (the latter calculated from the reported F statistic and degrees of η freedom).
Among sensitisers, the attended-ear advantage was 61 ms following neutral words (452 -391) and 134 ms following threatening words (480 -346), an increase of 73 ms.
The channel-by-word-type interaction within this group was significant, F(1, 6) = 9.59, p = .021, partial² = .61.
Among repressors, the corresponding η advantage fell from 96 ms after neutral words (504 -408) to 20 ms after threatening words (473 -453), a reduction of 76 ms.
The within-group interaction for repressors did not reach the conventional .05 level, F(1, 9) = 4.00, p ≈ .077, partial² = .31.
η
Accordingly, the central reported statistical result is the interaction between defensive group, preceding word type, and probe channel.
The numerical direction of the effect accords with the original predictions for both groups, but the separately tested effect within repressors did not reach the conventional .05 threshold.

These results show that the procedure produced a pattern of probe responses relevant to the original hypotheses; they do not, by themselves, establish a specific psychodynamic mechanism or provide a robust estimate of individual differences in defensive attention.
Inferential caution is warranted for additional reasons.
Very few probe observations contributed to each participant's condition means, and effect-size estimates from such a small study are unstable and may overstate the corresponding population effects.
The reported within-group tests were follow-up analyses of the three-way interaction; the available report does not document a multiplicity-adjustment strategy.
Their p values should therefore be read descriptively and with due caution rather than as independent confirmatory tests.
No modern reliability coefficients or item-level analyses can be calculated from the currently available summary statistics.
The auditory dissertation was submitted in March 1981.
The visual dot-probe article appeared five years later, in 1986 in (MacLeod et al., 1986)).
text.formatted: The visual dot-probe article appeared five years later, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">in 1986</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">in (MacLeod et al., 1986))</ref>.

text.text: Although the studies differed in sensory modality, participant samples, and the manner in which competing information was presented, they shared an important inferential arrangement: emotionally differentiated material was related to a neutral probe, and the participant's response to that probe was used to index the allocation of attention.

For clarity about the primary record, the auditory task discussed in this article was completed and reported in the UCL BSc dissertation submitted in 1981, and an archived copy of that document is available online (Halkiopoulos, 1981).
text.formatted: For clarity about the primary record, the auditory task discussed in this article was completed and reported in the UCL BSc dissertation submitted in 1981, and an archived copy of that document is available online <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Halkiopoulos, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: The 1986 acknowledgement refers to the work in the context of subsequent unpublished research; the dated dissertation makes the original design directly inspectable.
The relationship between the two experiments is documented in contemporary publications.

The acknowledgement in MacLeod et al. (1986, p. 15) states that my unpublished research "motivated the development of the current paradigm. " Eysenck, MacLeod, and Mathews (1987) subsequently described the auditory task and discussed a related visual procedure. Eysenck (1989, p. 147), in an account of work on selective processing, introduced the historical sequence as follows: "The first of a series of studies was carried out by Christos Halkiopoulos, in unpublished research."
text.formatted: The acknowledgement in <ref type="bibr">MacLeod et al. (1986, p. 15)</ref> states that my unpublished research "motivated the development of the current paradigm. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">" Eysenck, MacLeod, and Mathews (1987)</ref> subsequently described the auditory task and discussed a related visual procedure. <ref type="bibr">Eysenck (1989, p. 147)</ref>, in an account of work on selective processing, introduced the historical sequence as follows: "The first of a series of studies was carried out by Christos Halkiopoulos, in unpublished research."

text.text: Eysenck characterised the earlier findings as "potentially of great interest, because at last we have convincing evidence of threat avoidance by low-anxiety individuals and threat approach by high-anxiety individuals as originally proposed by Byrne".
He added: "Of course, it would be desirable to replicate such an important finding, and this has been done by MacLeod, Mathews, and Tata (1986)" (Eysenck, 1989, p. 147).
text.formatted: He added: "Of course, it would be desirable to replicate such an important finding, and this has been done by MacLeod, Mathews, and Tata (1986)" <ref type="bibr">(Eysenck, 1989, p. 147)</ref>.

text.text: These assessments are reported to document how the findings and subsequent research were understood at the time; they do not remove the empirical limitations considered in Section 5.

In particular, the original UCL experiment assessed defensive style rather than independently measuring trait anxiety. Mathews (1990, p. 459) offered a particularly direct account of the methodological transition:
text.formatted: In particular, the original UCL experiment assessed defensive style rather than independently measuring trait anxiety. <ref type="bibr">Mathews (1990, p. 459</ref>) offered a particularly direct account of the methodological transition:

text.text: In an initial unpublished experiment by a student of Michael Eysenck (C. Haliopoulos), high trait anxious Ss were found to detect tones in a dichotic listening tape more rapidly if these followed a threatening word.
Converting this to the visual modality, we found a similar effect in clinically anxious (GAD) Ss.
This retrospective description identifies the change of modality as part of the research sequence.

The original experiment had been completed at UCL under Norman Dixon's supervision and had classified participants by Ullmann's defensiveness-related scale; those distinctions remain relevant to interpretation.
In a later recollection reproduced in Borkovec's (2004) biographical chapter, Mathews described the exchange of ideas in these terms:
text.formatted: In a later recollection reproduced in <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Borkovec's (2004)</ref> biographical chapter, Mathews described the exchange of ideas in these terms:

text.text: Then Michael Eysenck made contact, and we picked up the idea for the dot probe method from his student, Chris Haliopoulos.
I certainly remember that being a really fun time.
(Andrew Mathews, quoted in Borkovec, 2004, p. 13.) The spelling of my name is preserved as printed in the cited source.
text.formatted: (Andrew Mathews, quoted <ref type="bibr">in Borkovec, 2004, p. 13.)</ref> The spelling of my name is preserved as printed in the cited source.

text.text: Read together with the earlier publications, these recollections contribute evidence about the route through which the auditory task became relevant to the development of the visual dot-probe method.
These published accounts are considered here for the historical information they provide.

They are consistent with the earlier auditory experiment forming one identifiable contribution to the development of the visual task, alongside other relevant conceptual and methodological influences.
As the next section explains, the two procedures also differ in important operational respects.
The aim is to describe that relationship accurately, rather than infer a single uninterrupted history for the many forms of attention-probe research.
The two tasks should not be regarded as operationally identical.

My auditory experiment used an explicitly attended speech stream, continuous shadowing, and occasional tones in one of two ears; the visual dot-probe task used spatially separated visual material followed by a target at one of the relevant locations.
The common feature is a more abstract methodological logic: a neutral probe response is used to make inferences about attention in the context of emotionally differentiated information.

In this sense, the auditory experiment constitutes an early documented implementation of a recognisably related emotional attentional-probe arrangement, and the visual task represents a consequential subsequent development.
This history is also compatible with the broader development of probe research.

The auditory and visual attention literatures supplied different techniques for manipulating selective attention, creating target signals, and interpreting reaction-time or electrophysiological differences.
The methodological history is best understood as one of partly converging lines of work rather than a single uninterrupted lineage.
What can be established with particular clarity in the present case is the design documented in 1981 and the later published acknowledgement of its contribution to the visual method.
>Methodological interpretation and limitations
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Methodological interpretation and limitations</head>

text.text: The 1981 study addressed a substantive question that remains of interest: whether emotionally threatening input changes the distribution of attention between channels in a way that differs across individuals.
The observed three-way interaction is compatible with such a possibility.

The accompanying directional pattern suggests that sensitisers devoted relatively more attention to the shadowed channel after threatening words, whereas repressors showed a reduced advantage for that channel.
However, probe reaction time is an indirect measure.
Differences can reflect perceptual selection, alerting, preparation, competing task demands, and response-related factors, and the original data cannot uniquely distinguish among these explanations.
The original reasoning was framed in terms of perceptual defence and repression.

Later theories of repressive coping proposed that vigilance and avoidance could occur at different stages of processing (Derakshan et al., 2007), but the present experiment did not measure a temporal sequence of such stages.
text.formatted: Later theories of repressive coping proposed that vigilance and avoidance could occur at different stages of processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Derakshan et al., 2007)</ref>, but the present experiment did not measure a temporal sequence of such stages.

text.text: It is therefore better to describe its findings as broadly compatible with hypotheses about defensive attention than as a direct demonstration of a vigilance-avoidance mechanism.
Several limitations are particularly important.
First, the analysed sample comprised only 17 students, making the estimates uncertain and the subgroup comparisons especially fragile.
Second, the small number of probe trials per condition limits the precision and potential reliability of reaction-time measures; a conventional psychometric reliability analysis is not available.

Third, the set of probed words was very restricted and not adequately matched across all potentially relevant properties, so differences in item features, acoustic realisations, and shadowing demands cannot be separated cleanly from emotional valence.
Fourth, the surviving description does not permit a detailed contemporary assessment of synchronisation, temporal intervals, counterbalancing, exclusion criteria, or trial-level data processing.
Fifth, the defensive-style grouping was not accompanied by independent measurement of trait anxiety.
The study was not preregistered, as would be expected for much contemporary experimental work; its original analyses are presented as historical results, not as a new confirmatory evaluation.
A further conceptual limitation is that one cannot infer the absence of response bias simply because the response was emotionally neutral.
The design reduced reliance on direct emotional judgements but did not eliminate every possible source of measurement bias.
These qualifications affect the strength of conclusions about the effects of threatening words, not the fact that the dissertation specified and implemented the method.
The later dot-probe literature offers an instructive perspective.
Reviews and measurement studies have identified limited internal consistency and test-retest reliability of some conventional probe-based bias indices (Kappenman et al., 2014; McNally, 2019).
text.formatted: Reviews and measurement studies have identified limited internal consistency and test-retest reliability of some conventional probe-based bias indices <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kappenman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">McNally, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: More recent task variants, including a dual-probe procedure, have been designed partly to improve psychometric performance (Grafton et al., 2021).
text.formatted: More recent task variants, including a dual-probe procedure, have been designed partly to improve psychometric performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grafton et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Any present-day implementation of the auditory task should benefit from these developments rather than reproduce the original 1981 protocol unchanged.
The case for studying emotional attentional bias in audition does not rest solely on the historical experiment.

Later investigators have examined spatial orienting towards emotional spoken words using auditory beep probes. Bertels, Kolinsky, and Morais (2010), for example, presented concurrent spoken words from spatially separated sound sources followed by a lateralised beep and reported emotion-related spatial effects. Asutay and Västfjäll (2015) likewise considered the ways negative emotion can guide auditory spatial attention.
text.formatted: Later investigators have examined spatial orienting towards emotional spoken words using auditory beep probes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bertels, Kolinsky, and Morais (2010)</ref>, for example, presented concurrent spoken words from spatially separated sound sources followed by a lateralised beep and reported emotion-related spatial effects. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Asutay and Västfjäll (2015)</ref> likewise considered the ways negative emotion can guide auditory spatial attention.

text.text: These studies demonstrate the feasibility and continuing relevance of auditory approaches, while involving procedures that are not simple replications of the original dichotic-shadowing task.

A contemporary research programme could systematically vary whether emotional information occurs in the explicitly attended or competing stream, the timing of probes relative to word onset, the emotional properties of naturalistic speech, and the stability of probe-derived attentional indices.

It could also compare behavioural reaction-time measures with electrophysiological measures of selective processing, extending the kind of comparison invited by the earlier work of Hink and Hillyard (1976).
text.formatted: It could also compare behavioural reaction-time measures with electrophysiological measures of selective processing, extending the kind of comparison invited by the earlier work of <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hink and Hillyard (1976)</ref>.

text.text: Larger item sets, repeated assessments, and independently validated stimuli would allow more reliable estimation of individual differences.

The 1981 UCL dissertation documented a specific experimental response to a long-standing problem in emotion research: how to investigate attentional consequences of threatening information without requiring participants to report the threatening material itself.
Its solution combined dichotic shadowing and emotionally differentiated speech with neutral tone probes delivered to either ear and an invariant speeded response.
The original findings were suggestive but limited, and their substantive interpretation requires caution.

The historical significance of the experiment lies primarily in the methodological configuration it established and its documented place in the subsequent development of emotional attentional-probe research.

Earlier probe methods form an important part of the broader history of attention; the 1981 experiment applied related measurement principles to a distinctive theoretical question and experimental arrangement.
The emergence of the visual dot-probe task in 1986 and later auditory variants illustrate the continuing adaptability of that general approach.
This history offers both a fuller account of the development of a widely used research method and a starting point for further work on emotion and auditory selective attention.
This article reports the descriptive statistics and statistical tests documented for a study completed in 1981 and reconstructs its methodology in the context of subsequent published work.
The original BSc dissertation is available via the OSF deposit identified in the references.
No new participants were recruited and no new participant-level statistical analysis was undertaken.

Numerical p values are stated to three decimal places where they can be obtained from the reported F statistics and degrees of freedom; partial ² for the three-way η interaction was calculated from those summary statistics.
Original recordings, complete trial-level data, and stimulus-level response records were not available for reanalysis when preparing this manuscript.
The experiment is therefore evaluated as an exploratory historical study.
Its place in methodological history is assessed separately from the reliability of its substantive empirical results.
